title: Old, Middle and New Kingdoms
description: Egyptian history peaks in three kingdoms (Old, Middle, New), separated by Intermediate Periods when the country split.

facts.text: In the Oxford History of Ancient Egypt’s chronology, the Old Kingdom ran from about 2686 to 2160 BCE, the Middle Kingdom from about 2055 to 1650 BCE and the New Kingdom from about 1550 to 1069 BCE.
The Old Kingdom was the age of the great pyramids at Giza; the Middle Kingdom began when Egypt was reunited; in the New Kingdom Egypt became an empire.
Between the kingdoms came the First, Second and Third Intermediate Periods, when the land was politically divided, often under local rulers in Upper and Lower Egypt.

title: Three thousand years
description: Ancient Egypt lasted about 3,000 years, from unification around 3100 to 3000 BCE to Roman rule in 30 BCE.

facts.text: Ancient Egyptian civilization lasted about 3,000 years, from unification around 3100 to 3000 BCE until Egypt became a province of the Roman Empire in 30 BCE.
Upper and Lower Egypt became one kingdom around 3100 to 3000 BCE: the Met dates unification to about 3100 BCE, and the Oxford History starts the First Dynasty about 3000 BCE.
Cleopatra, who died in 30 BCE, lived closer in time to the 1969 Moon landing than to the building of Khufu’s Great Pyramid, completed by the early 25th century BCE.

title: The Nile’s yearly flood
description: Summer rains in Ethiopia made the Nile flood Egypt each year, leaving fertile silt on fields in an almost rainless land.

facts.text: Egypt gets very little rain: a little over an inch a year at Cairo and less than an inch in Upper Egypt.
The Nile flooded Egypt each year, roughly from July to October, because of heavy summer monsoon rains far to the south in Ethiopia.
The Blue Nile, which rises in the Ethiopian highlands, plays the biggest part in bringing the Nile flood to Egypt.
As the flood drained away it left dark, fertile silt on the fields, a natural fertilizer that let Egypt support a dense population and prosperous cities.
A flood that was too low left some fields dry and could bring hunger; a flood that was too high could wipe out villages.
Egyptians believed the flood was a gift of the gods; if it was too great or too small, they blamed an angry river or a king who had neglected his duties, not the weather far to the south.

The Greek historian Herodotus, who visited Egypt in the 5th century BCE, called the Egypt the Greeks sailed to ‘the gift of the river’ (usually quoted as ‘the gift of the Nile’), meaning land built up by the Nile.

title: Black land, red land
description: Kemet, the narrow black land of the Nile valley, fed Egypt; Deshret, the red desert around it, was used for burials and guarded the borders.

facts.text: Egyptians called their country Kemet, ‘the black land,’ after the dark, fertile silt of the Nile valley.
Deshret, ‘the red land,’ was the Egyptian name for the hot, dry desert around the valley.
Between Cairo and Aswan, the Nile valley’s farmland is mostly 8 to 16 km wide, narrowing in places to a few hundred meters.
Egyptian cities could flourish only in the Nile valley, the Delta or desert oases, where people had water and good land.
The desert’s dry climate made it an ideal place for cemeteries.
Egypt had a favorable and secure location, bordered by deserts to the west and east, the Mediterranean Sea to the north and the First Cataract of the Nile at Aswan to the south.
Egypt was not isolated: it was a center for trade routes to and from western Asia, the Mediterranean and central Africa.

title: Farming by the flood
description: The Egyptian year ran in three seasons set by the Nile: flood, then plowing and sowing in the wet silt, then harvest and low water.

facts.text: The Egyptian year had three seasons of four months each: Akhet, the inundation; Peret, when the land emerged from the flood; and Shemu, when water was low.
When the floodwaters receded and left rich soil on the fields, planting and harvesting followed, then a dry season of low water until the next flood.
Egyptian farmers tilled with a wooden plow drawn by an ox or a donkey, and seed was sown from a funnel on the plow or trodden into the soil by sheep.
Egypt’s main crops were emmer wheat and six-rowed barley, along with lentils, beans, flax and onions.
Egyptian farmers cut their crops with sickles.
Early Egyptian farmers grew flax and wove it into linen.

title: The Nile as Egypt’s road
description: The north-flowing Nile and the north wind made a two-way road: drift north on the current, sail south with the wind, as far as the First Cataract.

facts.text: The Nile flows north through northeastern Africa into the Mediterranean Sea.
Egypt’s prevailing wind blew from the north, so boats going south, upstream, could sail with the wind behind them, while boats going north used the current and oars against the wind.
A wooden model riverboat from the tomb of the official Meketre at Thebes, from about 1985 BCE and now at the Met, shows twelve oarsmen rowing it downstream with the mast down.
The Nile was an important highway: the easiest way to travel, and essential for mining expeditions, trade, building projects and everyday travel.
The First Cataract at Aswan was a stretch of rock-strewn rapids that partly blocked the river, and it marked Egypt’s southern border.

title: The Two Lands
description: Egypt was two lands, Upper Egypt (the southern valley) and Lower Egypt (the Delta), each with its own crown, joined in the double crown.

facts.text: Upper Egypt was the southern Nile valley and Lower Egypt the northern Delta; the names follow the north-flowing river, so the south is upstream.
North of present-day Cairo, the Nile fans out into several branches, forming the Delta.
In late predynastic times, Upper Egypt and Lower Egypt were separate political lands.
The crown of Upper Egypt was white and cone-shaped; the crown of Lower Egypt was red and flat, with a rising back and a spiral curl in front.
Kings often wore the two crowns combined as the double crown, a symbol of Upper and Lower Egypt united under one king.
After unification, every Egyptian king held the title ‘King of Upper and Lower Egypt.’
No actual Egyptian royal crown has survived, so what the crowns were made of is not known for certain; we know them from works of art.

title: Egypt before the pharaohs
description: Farming villages appeared in Egypt by about 5000 BCE; Badarian potters and later towns followed, and Upper Egyptian culture spread north.

facts.text: By about 5000 BCE, villages in the Faiyum kept sheep, goats and pigs and grew emmer wheat, barley and flax.
Farming in Egypt only intensified after domesticated animals were introduced from Southwest Asia.
Around 4000 BCE, the Badarian farmers of Upper Egypt made thin-walled, well-fired, black-topped pottery that many regard as the best ever made in the Nile valley.
The Badarians also made ivory combs and spoons and flat stone palettes.
Before the kings, Egypt went from early farming communities to towns, and the culture of Upper Egypt spread north into Lower Egypt, probably through trade.
Boats are among the earliest designs painted on Egyptian Predynastic pots, which date to about 3500 to 3300 BCE.

title: Narmer and unification
description: Upper and Lower Egypt became one kingdom around 3100 to 3000 BCE. Tradition credits Menes; the Narmer Palette shows both crowns, but its meaning is debated.

facts.text: Egyptian tradition named Menes as the first king of unified Egypt, who joined Upper and Lower Egypt and founded Memphis, which became the capital.
Menes is legendary: scholars have tried, without settling it, to match him with early kings such as Narmer and Aha, and he may stand for several kings.
The Narmer Palette, a ceremonial palette found at Hierakonpolis in Upper Egypt and now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, shows Narmer in the white crown on one side and the red crown on the other.
The Narmer Palette dates to just before the First Dynasty and is one of the earliest examples of Egyptian relief sculpture.
Scholars disagree about the Narmer Palette: some read it as a record of Narmer conquering the north, others as a ritual statement of conquest rather than a real event.
Egypt’s political unity seems to have come gradually, through a shared culture and a series of conflicts over several reigns, rather than one single conquest.

title: Dynasties and dates
description: Egyptians counted years by reigns; Manetho grouped kings into 30 dynasties, which historians group into kingdoms. Dates before 664 BCE are approximate.

facts.text: Egyptians did not count years from one fixed starting point; they counted the years of each king’s reign.
The few surviving Egyptian king lists are broken in places, leave out some controversial rulers and list some rival dynasties as if they ruled one after another.
Around 300 BCE, the Egyptian priest Manetho wrote a history of Egypt in Greek that divided its rulers into 30 dynasties.
Manetho grouped kings into dynasties by factors such as family ties or the location of their main royal residence.
Manetho’s history survives only in fragments quoted by later writers, yet his 30 dynasties are still the basic framework of Egyptian history.
Historians group Egypt’s dynasties into larger periods: the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms and the Intermediate Periods between them.
Egyptian dates can be tied exactly to our calendar only from 664 BCE on; earlier dates are approximate, and different experts’ dates can differ by decades or more.

title: How the Nile made Egypt
description: River, flood, black land, guarding desert and the joining of two lands add up to one story of how Egypt began and why it lasted.

facts.text: Egypt’s favorable and secure location, guarded by deserts, sea and cataract, helped its civilization thrive for some 3,000 years.

title: What a pharaoh was
description: The Egyptian king judged, kept the gods content and set order in place of disorder; his divinity came from his office. The word pharaoh (per-aa, great house) meant the palace and was used for the king only from the New Kingdom.

facts.text: The word “pharaoh” comes from the Egyptian per-aa, “great house,” which originally meant the royal palace.
Egyptians began using per-aa for the king himself only in the New Kingdom, from the 18th Dynasty; later it became a respectful title.
An Egyptian text summing up the king’s role says he “is on earth for ever and ever, judging mankind and propitiating the gods, and setting order in place of disorder.”
The king’s divinity came from his office and was reaffirmed through rituals, but it was far below that of the major gods; he showed the gods to people and represented people to the gods.
The living king was identified with Horus, the falcon god, and at death the king became Osiris, god of the underworld.

title: Crook, flail and regalia
description: Royal regalia marked the office: the crook (the king as herdsman), the flail (meaning unclear, already on the Narmer Palette), the nemes headcloth, the uraeus cobra and the royal beard.

facts.text: Egyptian royal regalia included crowns, headcloths, the royal beard, an animal tail, sceptres, and the crook and flail.
The royal crook began as a herdsman’s staff, curved at one end, and became a sign of kingship through the idea of the king as herdsman of his people.
The meaning of the royal flail is unclear: it has been read as a herdsman’s whip, a symbol of birth, or a tool for gathering labdanum resin.
The flail already appears on the Narmer Palette and kept roughly the same shape throughout Egyptian history.
The god Osiris was shown holding a crook in one hand and a flail in the other.
The nemes was a royal headcloth: a folded cloth laid over the head, whose two lappets fell onto the chest.
The uraeus was the rearing cobra worn on the forehead of kings and gods; it was the goddess Wadjet, protector of Lower Egypt.

title: Viziers and scribes
description: The vizier was the chief administrator and judge under the king; the New Kingdom had two, for Upper and Lower Egypt. Provinces had their own officials, and government ran on writing that few could read.

facts.text: At the top of Egypt’s ranked hierarchy of officials was the vizier, the chief administrator and judge, who reported to the king.
As the king’s deputy, the vizier oversaw the treasuries and granaries, supervised officials, managed temple affairs and administered justice.
At first one vizier served all of Egypt; by the New Kingdom there were two, one for Upper Egypt based at Thebes and one for Lower Egypt based at Memphis.
Much of what we know about the vizier’s duties comes from inscriptions in the Theban tomb of Rekhmire, a vizier under Thutmose III.
By the Old Kingdom, Egypt was divided into provinces called nomes, each with its own officials.
Writing was the essential tool of Egyptian government, and about 99 percent of Egyptians could not read; texts urging the young to be scribes said the scribe commanded while the rest did the work.

title: Taxes without coins
description: Egypt taxed in goods and labor, stored grain in state granaries, set taxes by the flood height, and had no coins until the mid-first millennium BCE.

facts.text: Egypt’s economy was nonmonetary: the state’s core jobs were collecting, storing and redistributing produce, organizing labor and supervising legal matters.
For most of its history, Egypt taxed goods: officials collected dues in grain, textiles, labor, cattle and other commodities.
Taxes were often tied to farming, with a share of each field’s harvest set aside for state granaries; the state and temples held massive reserves of grain.
Metal coins came into use in Egypt only in the mid-first millennium BCE, introduced by foreign powers: the Persians and later the Macedonians.
Nilometers measured the height of the Nile flood, and a level that promised a strong harvest meant higher taxes.
In the Old Kingdom, the king toured the country every year or two on the “Following of Horus,” checking the provinces’ wealth and collecting taxes.
Egyptians below the rank of official could be called up by the state to work on public projects: tilling fields, quarrying, and building temples and tombs.

title: Egypt’s army
description: Early Egypt relied on local militias; horse, chariot and composite bow arrived in the Second Intermediate Period; New Kingdom chariots carried a driver and an archer.

facts.text: Before the Middle Kingdom, civil and military roles were not sharply separated: Egypt’s forces were local militias under their own officials and included foreigners.
In the Middle Kingdom, King Senusret III (also called Sesostris III) completed a chain of fortresses at the Nile’s Second Cataract in Nubia.
During the Second Intermediate Period, composite bows, new daggers and scimitars, and above all the horse and chariot transformed Egyptian warfare.
These new weapons brought Egypt, which had been technologically behind, up to the level of southwest Asia.
An Egyptian war chariot normally had a crew of two, a driver and an archer, and chariot bodies were light enough to be carried on a man’s shoulder.
The New Kingdom army was divided into infantry and chariot forces, and it recruited both Egyptians and foreign troops.

title: Ma’at: order and justice
description: Ma’at meant truth, justice and cosmic order, opposed to isfet (chaos). Keeping it was the king’s central duty, and the Tale of the Eloquent Peasant shows it applied to everyone.

facts.text: Ma’at was the Egyptian idea, and goddess, of truth, justice and cosmic order.
The goddess Ma’at was shown as a woman with an ostrich feather on her head.
The opposite of ma’at was isfet, disorder and chaos, and the king’s duty was to set order in place of isfet, as the sun god Re did.
Ma’at was the divine order set up at creation and reaffirmed each time a new king came to the throne.
New Kingdom temple reliefs show the king presenting a figure of Ma’at to the gods.
In the Middle Kingdom Tale of the Eloquent Peasant, a peasant named Khunanup is robbed of his donkeys and goods by Nemtinakht and appeals to the high steward Rensi.
In the tale, the king orders Rensi to keep the peasant talking without answering him, so his speeches can be written down, while secretly feeding him and his family.
The peasant appeals nine times; in the end the robber’s property is given to him.
In R. B. Parkinson’s translation the peasant says “Doing Truth is the breath of life”; “Truth” there renders ma’at, a word that rings through the tale.

title: Royal women
description: Queenly roles were shared: the Great King’s Wife, other wives and the king’s mother. Tiye rose without royal blood; Sobekneferu ruled as monarch.

facts.text: What we would call a queen’s role was often shared by several royal women at once, and much is unknown because Egyptian sources focus on the king.

The most important royal woman was the Great King’s Wife, the king’s chief wife and usually the mother of the next king; she ranked just after the king and was often shown beside him, usually smaller.
Kings also had other wives, including, at least from the New Kingdom, daughters of foreign rulers sent as part of diplomacy; the king’s wives usually lived in the royal harem.
The king’s mother could also play an important role and was occasionally shown beside the king.

Tiye, daughter of Yuya, a commander of the chariotry, was not of royal blood, yet she became Amenhotep III’s favored wife; he gave her prominence in state affairs, and her name appeared with his on official documents.
Scarabs commemorating Amenhotep III’s marriage to Tiye still survive.
Sobekneferu, who ruled at the end of the Middle Kingdom’s 12th Dynasty, is the first certainly attested woman to rule Egypt as monarch.

title: Hatshepsut
description: Hatshepsut went from great royal wife to regent to king (about 1473 to 1458 BCE), was shown with the king’s regalia, and was later partly erased for reasons still debated.

facts.text: Hatshepsut was the elder daughter of King Thutmose I; she married her half brother Thutmose II and was his great royal wife.
When Thutmose II died, about 1479 BCE, the throne passed to his young son Thutmose III, and Hatshepsut acted as regent.
By the end of Thutmose III’s seventh year as king, Hatshepsut had been crowned king herself, with a full set of royal titles.
Hatshepsut ruled as king in her own right from about 1473 to about 1458 BCE.

Hatshepsut was first shown as a typical queen; after a brief experiment mixing a female body with a king’s regalia, her official portraits showed a male body with kilt, crown or headcloth, and false beard.
Hatshepsut never explained why she took the throne or how she persuaded Egypt’s elite to accept her.
Scenes at Hatshepsut’s Deir el-Bahri temple claim that Thutmose I proclaimed her his heir and that the god Amun chose her mother to bear the new divine ruler.
Hatshepsut’s greatest monument was her temple at Deir el-Bahri, built as her funerary monument and dedicated to Amun-Re.
Late in Thutmose III’s reign, years after Hatshepsut’s death, her statues were broken and her name was removed from the official list of kings.

Why is debated: early scholars saw revenge; later Egyptologists argued Thutmose III wanted the succession to run from Thutmose I through Thutmose II to himself with no female king; a 2025 study argues the statues were ritually “deactivated,” as other kings’ statues were.
In the 1920s, archaeologists found many broken statues of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahri.

title: The royal court
description: Palaces were mud brick while temples were stone, so few survive; Malqata shows their painted splendor, and the harem could breed deadly plots.

facts.text: From the Old Kingdom on, stone was generally used for tombs and temples, the eternal houses of the dead and the gods, while mud brick was used for homes, even royal palaces.
Amenhotep III’s palace complex at Malqata, in western Thebes, is the best preserved Egyptian royal palace, and its walls, floors and ceilings were decorated with paintings.
One of Ramesses III’s secondary wives plotted to kill him and put her own son on the throne; the conspirators were put on trial.
A 2012 CT scan of Ramesses III’s mummy found a deep knife wound in the throat, indicating that the plotters did kill him.

title: How pharaohs held Egypt together
description: Ma’at gave the king his job; regalia announced it, officials and scribes ran it, grain taxes paid for it and the army defended it.

facts.text: Egyptian administration and law were not fully distinct, and both depended ultimately on the king.

title: Mastaba tombs
description: Before pyramids, Egyptians built mastabas: flat-topped, bench-shaped tombs over a shaft to a buried chamber, with a chapel above for offerings.

facts.text: Mastaba is the Arabic word for ‘bench.’
A mastaba was a rectangular tomb building with a flat roof and sloping walls, built of mud brick or, later, stone.
The mastaba was a form of tomb known in Egypt from the beginning of the dynastic era.
A deep shaft ran down from a mastaba to the underground burial chamber.
A mastaba had a chapel with an offering table and a false door, through which the dead person’s spirit could leave and enter the burial chamber.
Old Kingdom mastabas were used chiefly for burials of people who were not kings.
Late in the 5th dynasty, the palace administrator Perneb built a mastaba tomb at Saqqara; its facade and chapel were bought from Egypt in 1913 and rebuilt at the Met in New York.
In a mastaba such as Perneb’s, the burial chamber could not be reached after the funeral; relatives and priests came to the chapel above to pray and bring offerings.

title: Djoser’s Step Pyramid
description: Imhotep turned Djoser’s mastaba into six stone steps at Saqqara: Egypt’s first pyramid and the world’s oldest known monumental stone building.

facts.text: The Step Pyramid at Saqqara was built for Djoser, a king of the 3rd dynasty, and was the first Egyptian pyramid.
Djoser’s tomb began as a flat-topped mastaba and was changed into a pyramid of six steps.
The Step Pyramid rises in six stone steps, each smaller than the one below, to a height of about 60 m.
Djoser’s Step Pyramid was built entirely of stone, breaking with the older habit of building in mud brick along with stone.
The Step Pyramid is the oldest known monumental stone building in the world.
Imhotep, Djoser’s vizier, designed the Step Pyramid; his name and titles are carved on the base of a statue of Djoser now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.
Imhotep is often called the world’s first named architect.
Imhotep was later worshipped as a god of medicine, and the Greeks identified him with their healing god Asclepius.
Imhotep’s tomb has never been found.

title: Sneferu’s pyramids
description: Sneferu’s builders turned steps into smooth sides: Meidum was reworked, the Bent Pyramid changed angle when cracks appeared, and the Red Pyramid got it right.

facts.text: Sneferu was the first king of the 4th dynasty.
Sneferu’s pyramid at Meidum was built as a step pyramid and later reworked into a true, smooth-sided pyramid.
The Bent Pyramid at Dahshur, built for Sneferu, was the first pyramid designed from the start as a true pyramid.
The Bent Pyramid changes its angle about halfway up; the lower part is steeper than the upper part.
The Bent Pyramid’s lower part rises at 54 degrees and its upper part at 43 degrees.
The builders reduced the Bent Pyramid’s angle because cracks and structural faults appeared during construction.
The Red Pyramid at Dahshur, north of the Bent Pyramid, is the earliest tomb known to have been designed and built as a true pyramid throughout; its sides rise at 43 degrees.
Sneferu built three major pyramids: Meidum, the Bent Pyramid and the Red Pyramid.
Sneferu was succeeded by his son Khufu.

title: The Great Pyramid of Giza
description: Khufu’s Great Pyramid, about 146 m tall and built of some 2.3 million blocks, was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years.

facts.text: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for Khufu, second king of the 4th dynasty, and completed in the early 25th century BCE.
The Great Pyramid was originally about 146 m (481 feet) tall.
The Great Pyramid was the tallest human-made structure in the world for an estimated 3,800 years.
About 2.3 million stone blocks were cut, moved and fitted together to build the Great Pyramid.
Each side of the Great Pyramid’s base is about 230 m long.
Walking once around the Great Pyramid’s base, four sides of about 230 m each, covers about 920 m.
Polished limestone casing stones once made the Great Pyramid’s sides smooth and gleaming; erosion and the removal of most of them have left it shorter today.
The pyramids of Giza are counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, and they are the only one still standing.

title: Who built the pyramids
description: The builders’ cemetery, their skeletons and Merer’s logbook show the pyramids were built by Egyptian workers, called up in rotating crews and fed by the state, not by slaves.

facts.text: In 1990, a tourist’s horse stumbled on a mud-brick wall near the Giza pyramids, which led to the discovery of the pyramid builders’ cemetery.
The builders’ cemetery holds hundreds of small graves of laborers and larger tombs of overseers and craftsmen, with titles like ‘overseer of the side of the pyramid.’
Zahi Hawass, who excavated the builders’ tombs, said: ‘If they were slaves, they would not have been able to build their tombs beside their king’s.’
The builders’ skeletons show arthritis in the back and knees from heavy work, and broken arm and leg bones that healed after being splinted.
The pyramid builders were not slaves: they were Egyptians, many called up to serve rotating terms of work for the king under skilled craftsmen, and they were paid for their work.
In 2013, Pierre Tallet’s team found the oldest known inscribed papyri at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea, including the logbook of Merer, an inspector who led a crew under Khufu.
Merer reported to the noble Ankhhaf, Khufu’s half-brother, and his crew was supplied with food by the state.

title: Moving the stones
description: Blocks came by boat on the Nile, slid over wetted sand on sledges and went up ramps; exactly how the ramps worked is still debated.

facts.text: Merer’s logbook records his crew carrying limestone by boat from the quarries at Tura to Giza.
Egyptians moved heavy stone blocks on wooden sledges.
A wall painting in the tomb of Djehutihotep shows a man on the front of a sledge pouring water onto the sand in front of it.
A 2014 University of Amsterdam study found that the right amount of water halves the force needed to pull a sledge over sand.
Damp sand is about twice as stiff as dry sand, so it does not pile up in front of a sledge.
Archaeologists generally agree that ramps were used to raise blocks up the pyramids, but exactly how the ramps worked is still debated.
In 2018, researchers reported a steep ramp at the Hatnub alabaster quarry, flanked by two staircases with post holes, used to haul sledges up slopes of 20 percent or more.
The Hatnub ramp system dates back at least to the reign of Khufu, builder of the Great Pyramid.

title: The Great Sphinx
description: The Great Sphinx was carved from a block left in a quarry at Giza, most likely for Khafre in the 4th dynasty; it has a lion’s body and a king’s head.

facts.text: The Great Sphinx is about 73 m long and 20 m high, carved from a single mass of limestone.
When workers quarried a ditch in the Giza bedrock, they left a large block of limestone standing, and the Sphinx was carved from it.
The Sphinx has the body of a resting lion and a human head wearing a royal headdress.
Most scholars date the Great Sphinx to the 4th dynasty and credit it to King Khafre, whose face it probably shows.
Khafre built his own pyramid at Giza, and the Sphinx was likely part of his funerary complex.
Mark Lehner mapped the Sphinx and nearby temples stone by stone, and concluded that Khafre’s workers began shaping the Sphinx as they built his valley temple.
The Sphinx’s nose is missing, and drawings made before Napoleon’s troops reached Egypt already show it without one.
On the Dream Stela at the Sphinx, Thutmose IV (reigned about 1401–1391 BCE) recorded a dream in which the god promised to make him king if he cleared away the sand around the Sphinx.
Restoration work on the Sphinx possibly began in the reign of Thutmose IV.

title: The Lost City of the pyramid builders
description: South of the Sphinx lay the builders’ town: galleries for crews, bakeries, silos and meat enough to feed thousands.

facts.text: In 1988, Mark Lehner and AERA found a large settlement about 400 m south of the Sphinx, the base for building the pyramid complexes of Menkaure, Khafre and probably Khufu.
The Lost City of the Pyramids housed laborers, craftsmen, managers and administrators.
The settlement lies by a huge stone wall known in Arabic as Heit el-Ghurab, the ‘Wall of the Crow.’
Each long gallery in the Lost City may have housed a za, a crew of 40 men, while they served a term of compulsory work for the king.
The Lost City’s streets were lined with bakeries, kitchens and warehouses, and royal silos held grain for the bread and beer that fed the workforce.
Animal bones suggest that on average more than 4,000 pounds of cattle, sheep and goat meat were slaughtered daily for the builders; gallery workers ate mainly sheep and goats.

title: Why pyramids stopped
description: Pyramids advertised treasure. Later pyramids were smaller, robbers beat even Amenemhat III’s maze, and New Kingdom kings chose hidden tombs instead.

facts.text: The sheer size of a pyramid made it a target for tomb robbers.
Later pyramids were smaller and not as well built.
Amenemhat III, a 12th-dynasty king of the Middle Kingdom, built his pyramid at Hawara of mud brick with a white limestone casing.
Robbers still reached Amenemhat III’s burial at Hawara through its maze of passages and emptied the sarcophagi; Flinders Petrie concluded they had the plan from an informer.
Concern about tomb robbers led New Kingdom rulers to be buried in hidden tombs in the Valley of the Kings.

title: The pyramid age
description: From mastaba to Step Pyramid to true pyramid, then to hidden tombs: how and why Egyptians built pyramids.

facts.text: The pyramid shape may have been a stairway for the king’s spirit to climb to the heavens, the mound of creation, or the sun’s rays reaching down to earth.

title: Egypt’s many gods
description: Egyptians worshipped hundreds of gods, pictured as humans, animals or animal-headed humans, whose animal forms expressed their natures.

facts.text: Over the course of Egyptian history, hundreds of gods and goddesses were worshipped.
Egyptian gods took many forms: human forms, animal forms and mixed forms with an animal’s head on a human body.
Egyptians saw certain animals as forms of particular gods, and an animal’s traits said something about the god’s nature, such as the falcon for kingship.

Horus, who embodied divine kingship, was shown as a falcon or falcon-headed man; Anubis, who cared for the dead, as a jackal or jackal-headed man; Thoth, god of writing and wisdom, as an ibis, ibis-headed man or baboon; Hathor, linked with motherhood, as a cow or cow-headed woman.
Gods could be combined: Amun and Ra (Amon and Re) were joined as Amun-Ra, for more than a thousand years Egypt’s principal god.
The ankh, a cross topped by a loop, was the hieroglyph for “life,” and gods and pharaohs are often shown holding or offering it.

title: Ra’s daily journey
description: Egyptians believed the sun god Ra sailed the sky by day and the underworld by night, defeating the serpent Apophis to be reborn each dawn.

facts.text: Ra (Re) was the Egyptian god of the Sun and a creator god, and Heliopolis was the center of his worship.
Ra was often shown as a falcon-headed man with a sun disk on his head.
Egyptians believed Ra crossed the sky each day in a boat, his solar bark.
At night, Egyptians believed, Ra sailed another boat through the underworld, where he had to defeat the evil serpent Apophis (Apopis) to be born again for the new day.

title: The myth of Osiris and Isis
description: Seth killed Osiris; Isis gathered him, Anubis made him the first mummy, Horus avenged him, and Osiris ruled the dead, a promise every Egyptian shared.

facts.text: In the myth, Osiris ruled Egypt as king until his jealous brother Seth tricked him into a chest and threw it into the river; later Seth cut the body into 14 pieces and scattered them across Egypt.
Isis, Osiris’s wife, sought out and gathered the pieces of his body with her sister Nephthys, and she conceived their son, Horus.
In the myth, the jackal-headed god Anubis embalmed and wrapped Osiris’s body, making the first mummy.
Osiris lived on in the underworld as its ruler and judge.
Horus, son of Osiris and Isis, fought Seth, avenged his father and became king.
The living king was identified with Horus and the dead king with Osiris; later every Egyptian, not just kings, was linked with Osiris at death.
Seth was lord of the desert and a master of storms and disorder.

title: Temples as gods’ houses
description: Egyptian temples were homes for gods living in their statues, served daily by priests and seen by ordinary people mainly at festivals.

facts.text: An Egyptian temple was a house for its god or gods, and Egyptians believed a god lived within its statue in the temple’s shrine.
The sanctuary holding the god’s statue was the darkest, most enclosed part of the temple, with the highest floor level.
Each morning the high priest, acting for the king, opened the shrine, greeted the statue with hymns, dressed it in fine cloth and jewelry and presented food offerings.
The leftover offerings were divided among the priests as part of their wages.
Non-priests may have been allowed no farther than the temple’s open court.
At festivals, priests carried the god’s statue out in a barque, a portable shrine shaped like a boat, so ordinary people could glimpse the god.

title: Mummification: why and how
description: Egyptians preserved the body for the ka and ba; over about 70 days embalmers removed organs, dried the body in natron and wrapped it in linen.

facts.text: The earliest Egyptian mummies were made naturally: bodies buried in shallow pits in the desert sand were dried out by its heat.
Egyptians believed the ka and ba, the most important parts of a person’s soul, needed a well-preserved body they could recognize and return to; without it, they could not survive.
Mummification took about 70 days, and the Greek historian Herodotus also gave a figure of 70 days.
Embalmers removed the brain through the nose with a hooked metal tool, and it was often thrown away.
Through a cut in the side, embalmers removed the lungs, stomach, liver and intestines, which were embalmed separately and placed in canopic jars.
The heart was usually left inside the body, because Egyptians saw it as the center of knowledge and emotions.
The body was dried with natron, a natural salt, which was removed after about 40 days.
The body was then wrapped in layers of linen, often with amulets included in the wrappings.

title: The weighing of the heart
description: Egyptians believed the dead were judged by weighing the heart against the feather of Maat; Ammit ate a failed heart, the worthy reached the Field of Reeds.

facts.text: Egyptians believed that after death a person’s heart was weighed on scales against the feather of Maat, which stood for truth and right order.
In the judgment scene of Hunefer’s Book of the Dead, Anubis brings Hunefer in and supervises the scales, ibis-headed Thoth records the verdict and Horus presents him to Osiris.
Hunefer’s Book of the Dead, made for a royal scribe around 1275 BCE, is now in the British Museum.
Ammit, the Devourer, waited by the scales, with a crocodile’s front, a lion’s middle and a hippopotamus’s rear; if the heart failed, Ammit ate it and the dead person was denied the afterlife.
At the judgment the dead declared to each of 42 judges that they had not committed a particular wrong, a text now called the Negative Confession.
Those who passed could live in the Field of Reeds, imagined as a perfect version of Egypt, with clear rivers, bright sun and plentiful crops to harvest.

title: The Book of the Dead
description: A papyrus roll of spells for the afterlife, grown from the royal Pyramid Texts and the Coffin Texts, bought and personalized by those who could afford it.

facts.text: The Book of the Dead was a collection of spells placed in tombs to protect and help the dead in the afterlife; about 200 are known.
Its Egyptian title was “The Chapters of Coming Forth by Day”; “Book of the Dead” is a modern name.
Its spells included ones to keep the dead from losing their head or heart, and ones to protect them from snakes, crocodiles and insects on the journey.
Spell 125 of the Book of the Dead covers the judgment before Osiris and the Negative Confession.
Scribes copied the spells onto rolls of papyrus, often colorfully illustrated, and sold them for burials; no papyrus contains every spell.
A buyer could get a ready-made copy with blank spaces for the owner’s name, or pay more and probably choose the spells.
Written on papyrus rather than on tomb walls or coffins, the spells reached far more people, though fine illustrated copies were expensive.

The Book of the Dead grew out of older texts: the Pyramid Texts, written inside Old Kingdom pyramids for kings, and the Coffin Texts, written mostly on the coffins of Middle Kingdom officials and nobles.
The Book of the Dead was probably compiled in the 16th century BCE.

title: Animal mummies
description: Egyptians mummified pets, food, sacred animals and, by the million, animals bought as offerings to gods.

facts.text: Egyptian animal mummies were of four kinds: pets buried to accompany their owners, food for the afterlife, sacred animals linked with gods, and votive offerings.
Pilgrims bought mummified animals as offerings to gods, such as cats for Bastet, ibises for Thoth and crocodiles for Sobek.
Dedicating an animal burial seems to have counted as a pious act.
The Catacombs of Anubis at North Saqqara, dedicated to the god Anubis, held almost 8 million animal mummies, most of them dogs.
About 1.75 million sacred ibis mummies were buried at Saqqara and about 4 million at Tuna el-Gebel, offerings to the god Thoth.
Scanning hundreds of animal mummies, a University of Manchester team found that around a third contained no animal material at all.

title: Amulets: scarab and wedjat eye
description: The scarab stood for the reborn sun and rebirth; heart scarabs and the wedjat eye protected the living and the dead.

facts.text: Egyptians linked the dung beetle, or scarab, rolling its ball of dung with the god Khepri rolling the Sun across the sky.
Khepri, the scarab god, was linked with creation, rebirth and the morning sun.
Young beetles seemed to come out of the dung ball as if self-created, which linked the scarab with coming into being.
Scarabs were the most numerous Egyptian amulets, and most were made for the living.
Heart scarabs, placed with the mummy, carried a Book of the Dead spell telling the heart not to stand up as a witness against its owner.

The wedjat eye, Horus’s eye that Seth damaged in their fight and that was healed, was one of Egypt’s most popular amulets, used for protection by the living and the dead; wedjat means “the sound one.”

title: Preparing for eternity
description: Egyptians prepared for life after death step by step: mummy, Opening of the Mouth, spells, amulets and shabtis, then judgment.

facts.text: In the Opening of the Mouth ritual, priests used special tools to touch the mouth and eyes of the mummy or statue so the spirit could eat, drink, breathe and see.
Shabtis were small figures buried with the dead to do their work in the afterlife; by the end of the New Kingdom the ideal set had 365, one for each day of the year, plus overseers.

title: How hieroglyphs work
description: Hieroglyphs look like pictures, but most signs stood for sounds (consonants only); meaning signs such as determinatives showed what kind of word was meant.

facts.text: Hieroglyphs could stand for the objects they depict, but usually stood for sounds: signs for one, two or three consonants.
Egyptian hieroglyphs recorded mostly consonants; vowels were not written.
The number of hieroglyphic signs in regular use stayed at about 700 for more than 2,000 years.
The hieroglyph for ’sun’ could also serve for ’day’ or as the name of the sun god Re.
The house sign, also used for the sound pr, helped write the verb ’to go out’; an added sign of walking legs, a meaning sign called a determinative, marked the difference.
Hieroglyphs were usually written from right to left, and the direction the signs faced showed which way to read.
Hieroglyphic writing apparently arose in the late predynastic period, just before Egypt’s First Dynasty.

title: Papyrus: paper from a reed
description: Papyrus sheets were made from crossed strips of a marsh plant pressed so its own sap glued them, then pasted into rolls.

facts.text: The English word ’paper’ comes from papyrus, a reedy plant that grows along the Nile.
The papyrus plant grew abundantly in marshes and was long cultivated in the Nile Delta.
Besides writing material, papyrus was used to make rope, matting, sandals and boats.

A papyrus sheet was made from strips of the stem’s pith laid side by side, crossed at right angles by a second layer, dampened and pressed so the plant’s sap glued them, then hammered and dried in the sun.
Papyrus sheets were pasted together into rolls, usually of no more than 20 sheets.
The earliest known papyrus roll, from the First Dynasty tomb of the official Hemaka (about 2900 BCE), is blank.

title: Training a scribe
description: In a land where very few could read, scribes trained in school, above all in hieratic, and wrote with reed brushes and black and red ink.

facts.text: Literacy in ancient Egypt was probably well below 1 percent of the population: fewer than 1 in 100 people.
Young men enrolled in scribal schools to learn reading, writing and the basics of mathematics.
Scribes were trained in hieratic, a cursive form of hieroglyphs used on papyrus, potsherds and stone flakes; hieroglyphs were used for monuments and display.
A scribe’s palette had two inkwells and a slot for reed pens; the scribe chewed a reed’s end into a brush, dipped it in water and rubbed it on the ink cake.
Egyptian scribes wrote the main text in black ink and used red ink for titles or corrections.
Because most Egyptians could not read or write, scribes ranked above most people, and Egyptian texts said the scribe commanded while the rest did the work.

title: Egyptian numbers and fractions
description: Egyptians wrote numbers by repeating signs for 1, 10, 100 and 1,000, used unit fractions, and applied math to practical problems like measuring fields.

facts.text: Egyptians wrote numbers in a decimal scheme, with separate signs for 1, 10, 100, 1,000 and so on, each repeated as many times as needed.
In hieroglyphs, 1 was a stroke, 10 a cattle hobble, 100 a coil of rope and 1,000 a lotus flower.
Because each sign was repeated, 300 was written as three coils of rope, and 999 took 27 signs: nine each for 100, 10 and 1.
Egyptian scribes worked with unit fractions, those with 1 as the numerator, though they also used two-thirds.
The Rhind papyrus, now in the British Museum, was copied in the 17th century BCE from a text about two centuries older; it has a table of fractions for division and 84 problems.
Problems in the Rhind papyrus include sharing bread and beer as wages and measuring the areas of fields.
Herodotus wrote that a man who lost land to the river could report it; the king’s men measured the loss and lowered his tax, and Herodotus thought the Greeks learned land measuring from this.

title: Egypt’s 365-day calendar
description: The civil calendar had 12 months of 30 days plus 5 extra days; the rising of Sirius marked New Year, and without leap years the calendar drifted through the seasons.

facts.text: The Egyptian calendar was the first known calendar to use a year of 365 days, close to the solar year.
The Egyptian civil calendar had 12 months of 30 days each (360 days), plus 5 extra days at the end of the year, making 365.
Sirius, which Egyptians called Sothis, first rose just before sunrise at about the time the Nile flood began, and its rising signaled New Year’s Day.
Egyptians long believed that Sothis caused the Nile flood.
Sirius rose at intervals of 365.25 days, not 365, so without leap years the civil calendar slowly drifted through the seasons, a full cycle taking 1,460 years.

title: The medical papyri
description: Two medical papyri show Egyptian medicine: the Edwin Smith Papyrus, a chiefly practical casebook of injuries, and the Ebers Papyrus, full of remedies and spells.

facts.text: The Edwin Smith Papyrus, from about 1600 BCE, describes 48 cases of injuries, mainly to the head, neck and upper torso.
Each Edwin Smith case follows a set formula: a description of the injury, diagnosis, prognosis and treatment.
Each Edwin Smith case gives one of three verdicts: a condition the doctor will treat, one he will contend with, or one that cannot be treated.
The Edwin Smith Papyrus is written in hieratic script.
The Edwin Smith Papyrus is chiefly rational, with only one incantation in its injury cases; its treatments include bandaging and splinting.
The back of the Edwin Smith Papyrus holds magical spells and recipes, including one ’for making an old man into a youth.’
The Ebers Papyrus, dated about 1550 BCE, contains hundreds of magical formulas and folk remedies, for troubles from crocodile bites to toenail pain.
The Ebers Papyrus describes the heart as the center of the blood supply, with vessels running throughout the body.

title: Lining up buildings by the stars
description: Egyptians aligned buildings to the directions with star-sighting tools; one leading idea is that pyramid builders found north from two stars and a plumb line.

facts.text: The sides of the Great Pyramid are accurately oriented to the four cardinal points.
The merkhet, a bar with a plumb line, was used to measure the transits of stars; the bay, a forked stick, was used for alignment.
In 2000, Cambridge Egyptologist Kate Spence proposed that pyramid builders found north when a plumb line lined up the stars Kochab and Mizar around the unmarked celestial pole.
Spence noted that the small orientation errors of earlier and later pyramids track the slow drift of Kochab and Mizar relative to true north.
Temple reliefs show the king performing ’stretching the cord,’ a surveying rite, with Seshat, goddess of writing.

title: Stories on tomb walls
description: Tomb paintings such as Nebamun’s show daily life as the owner wished to be remembered and hoped to live after death: vivid, but idealised and made for the wealthy.

facts.text: Nebamun was a scribe in charge of grain at Thebes; paintings from his tomb chapel, from about 1350 BCE, are in the British Museum.
In his fowling scene, Nebamun stands on a small papyrus boat with a throw-stick and three herons, his wife behind him, his daughter below and his cat catching birds.
Other Nebamun scenes show scribes recording his geese and cattle, and inspectors assessing a grain field for tax.
Tomb paintings recorded how the dead person wanted to be remembered and the life they hoped to have in the afterlife.
Tomb paintings were idealised and paid for only by the wealthy, so they do not show how most Egyptians lived.

title: Jewelry, faience and glass
description: Egyptian jewelry paired gold with carnelian, turquoise and lapis lazuli, or with faience and glass made to imitate them; faience came first, glass much later.

facts.text: Egyptian jewelry is dominated by gold, generally set with three colors: carnelian, turquoise and lapis lazuli, or glassy pastes imitating them.
Egyptian jewelry included diadems, necklaces, pectorals, amulets, pendants, bracelets, earrings and rings.
The designs of Egyptian jewelry were largely symbols with precise names and meanings, closely linked to hieroglyphic writing.
Faience, made from silica, soda or potash and lime and colored by a little copper or cobalt, was made in Egypt from about 4000 BCE.
Faience and glass were made into objects desired by all levels of Egyptian society.
Glassmaking began in Egypt in the New Kingdom, about 1500 BCE, some 2,500 years after faience: raw glass was made first, then reheated and shaped.

title: The Pyramid Texts
description: The Pyramid Texts, first carved inside the pyramid of Unas in the 24th century BCE, are Egypt’s oldest surviving religious writings: spells and prayers for a dead king’s afterlife.

facts.text: Unas, last king of the 5th Dynasty, who flourished in the 24th century BCE, was the first pharaoh to inscribe the inside of his pyramid, at Saqqara, with the Pyramid Texts.
The Pyramid Texts are prayers, hymns and spells meant to protect a dead king or queen and ensure life and sustenance in the hereafter.
The Pyramid Texts are the oldest surviving body of Egyptian religious and funerary writing.
Pyramid Texts are found in several 5th- and 6th-Dynasty pyramids at Saqqara, of which Unas’s is the earliest.

title: Homes of mud brick
description: Egyptians built houses and even palaces of sun-dried Nile mud brick, kept them cool with high windows and roof vents, and saved stone for tombs and temples.

facts.text: Egyptian mud bricks were made of Nile mud, a mix of clay and sand, sometimes with bits of straw or animal droppings; it was pressed into rectangular molds and dried in the sun.
Mud brick and wood were the standard materials for Egyptian houses and palaces throughout the Dynastic period, even for royal palaces.
From the Old Kingdom on, Egyptians generally used stone for tombs, the eternal homes of the dead, and for temples, the eternal homes of the gods.
Most ancient Egyptian towns were lost because they stood in the cultivated, flooded Nile valley, while many temples and tombs survived because they were built on ground the flood did not reach.
Egyptian houses had windows placed high to reduce sunlight, and hooded vents on the roof to catch the breeze.
The house of the vizier Nakht at Tell el-Amarna had at least 30 rooms, with separate apartments for the master, his family and his guests, plus bathrooms and lavatories.

title: Bread and beer
description: Bread and beer, both made from grain, were the staples of the Egyptian diet; beer was thick and nourishing, and food rations served as pay.

facts.text: Bread and beer were the staples of the ancient Egyptian diet, eaten and drunk every day.
Egyptian bread was made mainly with emmer wheat and baked in different shapes, including flat loaves like pita and tall conical loaves.
Making bread and making beer were closely related in ancient Egypt, since both used basically the same ingredients.
Egyptian beer was thick and cloudy, probably weaker in alcohol than modern beer, and an important source of nutrition rather than just a treat.
Egypt did not use coins or paper money, so workers and household staff were often paid in food rations.

A model bakery and brewery from the tomb of the official Meketre, made about 1981 to 1975 BCE and now at the Met, shows men crushing grain with pestles, women grinding it into flour and a basket of conical loaves.
Heavy tooth wear is the most common dental condition in ancient Egyptian remains, blamed on a coarse diet made rougher by sand, mostly wind-blown, in their staple food, bread.

title: Linen and eye paint
description: Egyptians dressed mainly in linen, and both men and women wore eye paint, which may also have had practical uses.

facts.text: Linen, made from flax, was the chief textile of ancient Egypt; wool was used more rarely, for example in warm cloaks.
Egyptian men wore a short skirt tied at the waist, and women wore a sheath-like gown from the ankles to just below the breasts.
Egyptian men and women both wore cosmetics, focused on the eyes: green eye shadow of powdered malachite and black or gray eyeliner.
One ingredient of dark Egyptian eye paint was galena, a lead sulfide mineral.
Egyptians considered eye paint attractive and pleasing to the gods, and also thought it good for health, keeping off disease-carrying flies and blocking the sun's glare.

In a 2010 lab study, French chemists found that lead compounds from Egyptian eye makeup raised nitric oxide output, which helps the immune system fight bacteria, by up to 240 percent in human skin cells.
Lead is toxic, and health agencies such as the US FDA warn today that lead-containing kohl can cause lead poisoning.

title: Growing up in Egypt
description: Egyptian children wore the sidelock of youth; only elite children had a chance at schooling, and most learned by working from a young age.

facts.text: Egyptian art often shows children unclothed, wearing the sidelock of youth, a single plait of hair also called the Horus lock, and with a finger to the mouth.
Only children from elite and royal families had the chance of some schooling; most learning was by apprenticeship, and girls' education centred on home life with their mothers.
Egyptian children worked from a young age; fingerprints in clay moulds for amulets show that children as young as ten worked in workshops.

title: Women's legal rights
description: Egyptian women could own property, make contracts and go to court in their own name, but society was not equal.

facts.text: From the Old Kingdom on, an Egyptian woman's formal legal status was nearly identical to a man's: she could own, buy and sell property, make contracts, bring or face court cases and act as a witness in her own name.
Britannica describes Egyptian women's legal status as only marginally inferior to that of men.
In her will, Naunakhte, a woman of the tomb builders' village of Deir el-Medina, excluded the children who had not cared for or supported her in old age; her property was separate from her husband's.
Socially, Egyptian women and men were not equal: women seldom held paid public posts, usually earned less and depended on family, and rarely served as witnesses to legal documents.

title: Cats in Egypt
description: Cats protected Egypt's grain, were loved as pets and were linked to the goddess Bastet.

facts.text: The ancient Egyptian word for cat was miu or miit, meaning 'he or she who mews'.
Cats hunted the rodents that threatened Egypt's grain and spread disease, and killed dangerous animals such as snakes and scorpions; pest control was the main reason cats were domesticated.
Egyptian art shows cats wearing collars and lurking under chairs, like household pets today.
Bastet was worshipped as a lioness and later as a cat, often shown as a woman with a cat's head, and was a goddess of the home, fertility, joy and the protection of children.
Bastet's home city was Bubastis in the Nile Delta, and Egyptians wore small cat figures as amulets, probably because of her.
Herodotus wrote that when a cat died a natural death, everyone in the household shaved their eyebrows; when a dog died, they shaved their head and whole body.
Diodorus of Sicily, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE, wrote that he saw an Egyptian crowd kill a Roman who had accidentally killed a cat.

title: Games and music
description: Egyptians played board games such as senet and mehen and made music with harps, flutes, singers and the sistrum.

facts.text: Senet was played on a board of 30 squares in three rows of ten; two players raced their pieces, usually five to seven each, to the end, moving by throwing casting sticks or bones.
Senet's last squares were special: one marked 'good' gave a free turn, and a water hazard square knocked a piece off the board.
Archaeological and artistic evidence suggests senet, one of the earliest known board games, was played as early as about 3100 BCE, more than 5,000 years ago.
Wealthy Egyptians played senet on ornate boards, while people with less scratched grids onto stone, tables or the floor; Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertari were fans.
In the New Kingdom, senet, whose name means 'passing', became associated with the journey to the afterlife.
Another early Egyptian game, mehen, was played on a spiral board shaped like a coiled snake, with lion-shaped pieces; its exact rules are unknown.
Harps, flute players and singers were the most common Egyptian musical ensemble, performing at festivals, banquets, funerals and temple rituals.
The sistrum was a rattle with loose crossbars, often hung with jingles, shaken in Egyptian temple rituals, especially in the worship of the goddess Hathor.

title: Work and trades
description: Nearly all Egyptians farmed; craftsmen worked beside them, pay came as rations, and the Satire of the Trades mocked every job but the scribe's.

facts.text: In the Satire of the Trades, a father taking his son to scribal school mocks other jobs: the potter is covered with earth, the barber wears out his arms, the fisherman works among crocodiles and the washerman handles filth.
The Satire of the Trades probably dates to the Middle Kingdom, and students were still copying it as a writing exercise centuries later, in the New Kingdom.
Egyptologists debate whether 'satire' is the right word for the text, given how starkly realistic its descriptions are.
Nearly all ancient Egyptians worked in agriculture and were probably tied to the land.
In theory all land in Egypt belonged to the king, though people living on it could not easily be removed, and some land could be bought and sold.
Egyptian craftspeople raised their techniques, many of which first came from Asia, to extraordinary levels of perfection.

title: Deir el-Medina
description: The New Kingdom village of the royal tomb builders, whose ostraca and papyri record daily life and the first recorded strike.

facts.text: Deir el-Medina was a New Kingdom village of the craftsmen, and their families, who cut and decorated the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings.
Researchers have recovered tens of thousands of written documents from Deir el-Medina, most dating from about 1275 to 1075 BCE.
In some periods most men at Deir el-Medina could read and write, while literacy across Egypt as a whole is estimated at only about 1 or 2 percent.
Ostraca, flakes of limestone and pieces of broken pottery, were used especially by Egyptians for writing and sketching, as an alternative to papyrus.

A limestone ostracon from Deir el-Medina, now in the British Museum, records workmen's absences over 280 days of Year 40 of Ramesses II, with reasons such as illness, brewing beer and embalming a relative.
In Year 29 of Ramesses III, about 1157 BCE, Deir el-Medina's tomb workers, whose grain rations were late, stopped work, shouted 'We are hungry!' and sat behind a temple: the first recorded strike.
The scribe Amunnakht recorded the strike on a papyrus now in the Museo Egizio in Turin; the grain was paid, but the workers struck again.

title: How we know daily life
description: Ordinary Egyptian life is known from clues such as teeth, fingerprints, lost towns and the everyday writing of Deir el-Medina.

facts.text: Deir el-Medina's thousands of papyri and ostraca are an invaluable source on the workers' daily lives, showing details rarely seen anywhere else in Egypt.

title: The Hyksos
description: Rulers of foreign lands from Southwest Asia held northern Egypt from Avaris, brought the horse and chariot, and were driven out by Ahmose, who began the New Kingdom.

facts.text: ‘Hyksos’ is the Greek form of an Egyptian title, heqa khasut, meaning ‘rulers of foreign lands.’
For generations before the Hyksos kings, people from Southwest Asia (the Levant) had been settling in the eastern Nile Delta.
From their capital at Avaris in the eastern Delta, the Hyksos ruled much of Lower Egypt as the 15th Dynasty for about a century.
Many scholars now think the Hyksos rose to power from within, as leaders at Avaris gained power while the pharaohs’ authority declined, rather than by a sudden invasion.
The Hyksos introduced new technology to Egypt, including the horse and chariot, the composite bow and improved metal weapons.
Egypt adopted the Hyksos’ horse-drawn chariot and composite bow, advantages that later helped it build an empire.
Kamose of Thebes campaigned against the Hyksos, and his successor Ahmose captured Avaris and drove them out.
Ahmose, who reigned about 1550 to 1525 BCE in the Oxford History’s chronology, founded the 18th Dynasty and so began the New Kingdom.
Later Egyptian texts vilified the Hyksos, yet they had ruled as pharaohs and appear as legitimate kings in the Turin king list.
In the Oxford History’s chronology, the Second Intermediate Period ran from about 1650 to 1550 BCE.

title: An Egyptian empire
description: After the Hyksos, New Kingdom kings built buffer zones that grew into an empire, from Nubia's gold to the Euphrates.

facts.text: Ahmose understood that the Hyksos had grown so strong because earlier Egyptian kings had allowed them to.
After the Hyksos were driven out, Ahmose and his successors pushed Egypt’s borders outward, creating buffer zones in Nubia to the south and Canaan to the north.
Later pharaohs, most notably Thutmose III, expanded those buffer zones into an empire.
In the New Kingdom Egypt conquered all of Nubia and controlled the Nile as far as the Fourth Cataract.
Gold from the Nubian deserts was greatly prized by the Egyptians.
Egypt ran New Kingdom Nubia through viceroys, who headed its administration and oversaw the collection of tribute.
Thutmose I campaigned through Syria as far as the Euphrates River.

title: Karnak
description: Karnak at Thebes, Egypt's largest temple complex, was the house of Amun-Re and grew rich on the New Kingdom's victories.

facts.text: Karnak was built up over nearly 2,000 years, from the Middle Kingdom to the Ptolemaic period, as ruler after ruler added to it.
Karnak, on the east bank of the Nile at Thebes (modern Luxor), is the largest temple complex in Egypt, the great temple of the state god Amun-Re.
Amun’s name meant ‘the Hidden One,’ and his image was painted blue to show that he was invisible.
Amun was the god of Thebes.
After the Theban victory over the Hyksos and the creation of an empire, Amun’s standing and the wealth of his temples grew.
From the New Kingdom on, Amun’s temple at Karnak was among the largest and wealthiest in the land.
Karnak’s Great Hypostyle Hall, called one of the wonders of antiquity, has 134 columns holding up its roof.

title: The Valley of the Kings
description: New Kingdom kings hid rock-cut tombs in a desert valley at Thebes, with temples built apart; almost all were robbed anyway.

facts.text: Thutmose I is thought to have been the first king to cut his tomb in the Valley of the Kings at Thebes, probably for greater security.
Fearing for the safety of their rich burials, kings of the 18th, 19th and 20th Dynasties hid their rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings, a narrow valley in the western hills at Thebes.
Above the Valley of the Kings rises a peak called the Qurn, whose shape may have reminded Egyptians of a pyramid.
New Kingdom kings’ mortuary temples were built separately, at the edge of the farmland, away from their hidden tombs.
A typical tomb in the Valley of the Kings was a corridor descending into the rock, interrupted by deep shafts (perhaps to stop robbers or to catch floodwater), leading to a burial chamber.
Virtually all the tombs in the Valley of the Kings were emptied in ancient times; Tutankhamun’s is the famous one that escaped pillage.

title: Thutmose III
description: Thutmose III won at Megiddo by a bold route, fought 17 campaigns, raised conquered princes at court and turned buffer zones into an empire.

facts.text: The obelisks called Cleopatra’s Needles, in New York’s Central Park and in London, were first set up by Thutmose III before the sun temple at Heliopolis and have nothing to do with Cleopatra.
In the Oxford History’s chronology, Thutmose III reigned about 1479 to 1425 BCE.
Thutmose III reigned about 1,400 years before Cleopatra, who died in 30 BCE.
Thutmose III became king as a boy, and Hatshepsut ruled as king beside him until her death in his 22nd year.
Almost as soon as his sole rule began, Thutmose III set out on a campaign into the Levant.
At Megiddo, Thutmose III rejected the safer routes and led his army along a narrow path over the mountain, surprising the enemy.
Megiddo fell after a siege of several months (sources give seven or eight), and the spoils included hundreds of chariots and more than 2,000 horses.
Thutmose III led 17 military campaigns in all.
The sons of conquered rulers were sent to Egypt as hostages and educated at court, so they could later go home to rule with Egyptian outlooks and sympathies.
Thutmose III had the record of his campaigns carved on the walls of the temple of Amun at Karnak.

title: Akhenaten and the Aten
description: Akhenaten raised the sun disc Aten above Amun, built Akhetaten (Amarna) and attacked Amun's name; whether it was monotheism is debated, and it did not outlast him.

facts.text: In the Oxford History’s chronology, Amenhotep IV, later called Akhenaten, reigned about 1352 to 1336 BCE.
Akhenaten raised the cult of the Aten, the sun’s disc, above the worship of most other gods, including Amun.
The Aten was not shown in human form but as the disc of the sun itself, bathing the king in its rays.
Amenhotep IV changed his name to Akhenaten, meaning ‘beneficial to the Aten.’
Akhenaten built a new capital on an empty site on the east bank of the Nile: Akhetaten, ‘Horizon of the Aten,’ known today as Amarna.
From his fifth year as king, Akhenaten set out to erase Amun’s name and image from monuments, causing widespread destruction in many temples.

Early Egyptologists called Akhenaten the world’s first monotheist; many scholars now describe his religion as monolatry, the worship of one god in preference to all others, and note it drew on other gods, so the question is still debated.
About four years after Akhenaten’s death, the court returned to Thebes and Akhetaten was abandoned.
After Akhenaten, Amun was restored as king of the gods, and the Aten religion quickly disappeared.

title: Nefertiti
description: Akhenaten's queen had an unusually royal role in art; her bust was found at Amarna in 1912, and whether she later ruled is debated.

facts.text: Nefertiti, Akhenaten’s queen, worshipped the Aten alongside him and was shown at the same scale as the king in religious scenes.
Some scenes show Nefertiti smiting Egypt’s enemies, a motif previously reserved for the pharaoh.
Nefertiti’s name is usually translated ‘a beautiful woman has come.’
On 6 December 1912, a German expedition led by Ludwig Borchardt found a painted limestone bust of Nefertiti in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Amarna.
Nefertiti’s bust is displayed in the Neues Museum in Berlin.
Only the bust’s right eye has an inlay; the empty left eye and its unfinished state suggest to many that it was a sculptor’s model kept in the workshop.
Some scholars think Nefertiti ruled beside Akhenaten as co-regent, or even as king under another name; others disagree, and the evidence is not conclusive.

title: The voyage to Punt
description: Egypt sailed the Red Sea to Punt for incense, gold and baboons, carrying ships across the desert; Punt's location is still debated.

facts.text: From Punt, Egyptian expeditions brought back incense, gold, leopard skins and living baboons.
Expeditions to Punt are recorded at least as early as the reign of Pepi II, about 2200 BCE.
Hatshepsut sent a famous expedition to Punt and had it recorded on the walls of her temple at Deir el-Bahri.
Excavations at Wadi Gawasis on the Red Sea show that Egyptians built ships by the Nile, took them apart, carried them across the desert and reassembled them on the coast for voyages to Punt.
Caves at Wadi Gawasis held ship timbers, rope and cargo boxes inscribed ‘wonders of Punt,’ from roughly 4,000 years ago.
Punt lay somewhere in the southern Red Sea region, and scholars have debated its location for more than 150 years; the leading candidates include the Horn of Africa and southern Arabia.
Chemical (isotope) signatures in two New Kingdom baboon mummies suggest the animals most likely came from Eritrea, Ethiopia or Somalia; the researchers call the result provisional.

title: The Amarna Letters
description: Clay tablets in Akkadian cuneiform show great kings writing to the pharaoh as brothers and vassals begging for his attention.

facts.text: The Amarna Letters, clay tablets, were discovered by chance at Tell el-Amarna in 1887 by a local woman.
There are 382 known Amarna tablets.
The Amarna Letters are cuneiform tablets written mostly in Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the day.
The Amarna Letters date to the reigns of Amenhotep III and Akhenaten.
The great kings of Babylonia, Assyria, Mitanni and the Hittites wrote to the pharaoh as equals and called him ‘brother.’
Letters from the great kings are often preoccupied with the exchange of gifts and with royal marriages.
Tushratta, king of Mitanni, complained that gold statues he had been promised arrived as gold-plated wood.
A vassal ruler of Gezer wrote to the pharaoh: ‘I fall at the feet of the king, my lord, my god, my Sun, seven times and seven times.’
Letters from vassal rulers in Syria and Canaan deal with local political and military troubles and often complain that the Egyptian court is not paying attention.

title: The New Kingdom story
description: From Hyksos rule to empire, Amun's wealth, hidden royal tombs and Akhenaten's short-lived revolution.

facts.text: In the New Kingdom, Theban kings drove out the Hyksos and built an empire, and Amun and his temples grew rich; then Akhenaten raised the Aten above Amun, a revolution that did not outlast him.

title: Tutankhamun, the boy king
description: A minor New Kingdom king who died young, famous because his small tomb survived nearly intact with its gold.

facts.text: Tutankhamun reigned about 1333 to 1323 BCE, in the New Kingdom; he became king at about nine and died at about 19.
Tutankhamun was born Tutankhaten, a name including the Aten, Akhenaten’s god; as king he became Tutankhamun, a name including Amun.
Under Tutankhamun, a decree restored the temples, images, priests and privileges of the old gods after Akhenaten’s reign.
How Tutankhamun died is debated: a 2010 study found malaria parasites and proposed malaria with bone disease, others point to a broken leg; neither is certain.
Tutankhamun’s small tomb, hastily converted for him and later sheltered by rock chippings from a later tomb, was the only royal tomb in the valley to largely escape plundering.
Tutankhamun’s mummy lay in a nest of three coffins, the innermost of solid gold, and wore a golden portrait mask.
Tutankhamun’s tomb held more than 5,000 objects.
But for his tomb, Tutankhamun has little claim to fame, yet he is better known than his longer-lived, better-documented predecessors and successors.

title: Ramesses the Great
description: Ramesses II reigned 66 years and put up more monuments and statues than any other pharaoh, borrowing older ones too.

facts.text: Shelley’s sonnet “Ozymandias,” published in 1818, is about a ruined statue of Ramesses II, whose boastful inscription stands amid empty desert.
Ramesses II, son of Seti I, reigned from 1279 to 1213 BCE, 66 years, one of the longest reigns in Egyptian history, and had more than 100 children, outliving many of them.
Ramesses II’s building included the Ramesseum, the two temples at Abu Simbel, a new capital called Per-Ramessu, and work on Karnak’s Hypostyle Hall and at Abydos.
Ramesses II erected more monuments and statues than any other pharaoh.
A statue in Turin’s Museo Egizio, made for an earlier king, probably Amenhotep II, was recarved to look like Ramesses II and given his name on the belt.
A 7.25-ton granite fragment of a Ramesses II statue from the Ramesseum, now in the British Museum, inspired Shelley’s “Ozymandias” as it was about to reach England in 1818.

title: Abu Simbel
description: Ramesses II’s two cliff temples at Abu Simbel, and their 1960s rescue from the Aswan High Dam’s lake.

facts.text: On about February 22 and October 22, the first rays of the morning sun run the length of Abu Simbel’s great temple and light its inner shrine.
Ramesses II built two temples at Abu Simbel: a great temple to the sun gods Amon-Re and Re-Horakhte, and a smaller one for Nefertari and the goddess Hathor.
Four seated figures of Ramesses II, each 20 metres tall, flank the great temple’s entrance; the smaller temple has 10.5-metre statues of the king and queen.
The Aswan High Dam’s reservoir threatened to flood Abu Simbel, and in 1960 UNESCO launched an international campaign to save the monuments of Nubia.
Between 1963 and 1968, with funds from more than 50 countries, both temples were cut into some 16,000 blocks and rebuilt more than 60 metres higher.

title: Kadesh and the first peace treaty
description: The Battle of Kadesh ended in a draw that Ramesses sold as victory, and led to the oldest surviving peace treaty.

facts.text: Around 1274 BCE (Britannica says 1275), Ramesses II fought the Hittites under King Muwatallis at Kadesh, on the Orontes River in Syria.
At Kadesh, false Hittite deserters misled Ramesses, and a surprise Hittite attack scattered his army; it was one of the largest chariot battles ever fought.
Ramesses regrouped and counterattacked, and Kadesh ended in an honorable draw: neither side won outright, and he did not take the city.
Ramesses claimed Kadesh as a great victory, and his temple reliefs show him single-handedly defeating the enemy.
Years after Kadesh, Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III made peace; theirs is the oldest known peace treaty whose text survives.
The Egyptian-Hittite treaty was made as between equal great powers, and its promises were reciprocal.
Both versions of the treaty survive: the Egyptian one on temple walls at Karnak, the Hittite one on a clay tablet from their capital, Hattusa.
A replica of the treaty hangs at UN Headquarters, near the Security Council Chamber.

title: Khufu
description: The builder of the Great Pyramid is known from few records and one tiny ivory statuette.

facts.text: Khufu, called Cheops by the Greeks, was the second king of the 4th Dynasty, son and successor of King Sneferu, and built the Great Pyramid at Giza.
Few written sources about Khufu’s life remain.
The only known statue of Khufu bearing his name is an ivory statuette 7.5 cm tall, found by Flinders Petrie at Abydos in 1903, wearing the crown of Lower Egypt.
The statuette’s head was knocked off during the dig and lost for three weeks, until Petrie’s team found it by sifting the excavated dirt.
Herodotus, writing some 2,000 years after Khufu, called his and Khafre’s reigns 106 years of oppression, but in Egypt Khufu was remembered as a wise ruler.

title: Seti I
description: Seti I, father of Ramesses II, left the finest reliefs at Abydos, a selective king list and a fully decorated tomb.

facts.text: Seti I, son of Ramesses I and father of Ramesses II, reigned about 1290 to 1279 BCE in the 19th Dynasty.
Seti I restored Egypt’s power abroad, fighting in Palestine and Syria and at least once against the Hittite king Muwatallis.
Ramesses II became far more famous, but scholars often regard his father Seti I as the better ruler.
Seti I’s temple at Abydos has reliefs among the finest in any Egyptian temple, many still with their original color.
A wall in Seti I’s Abydos temple shows Seti and his son Ramesses honoring a list of 76 kings, from Menes to Seti himself.
The Abydos King List leaves out rulers such as Hatshepsut, Akhenaten and Tutankhamun.
Seti I’s tomb, KV17, is one of the longest in the Valley of the Kings and the first decorated with a complete program of religious texts.
Giovanni Belzoni found Seti I’s tomb in 1817, with its wall paintings still looking fresh.
Seti I’s alabaster sarcophagus is now in Sir John Soane’s Museum in London.

title: Cleopatra VII
description: The last Ptolemaic ruler: Macedonian Greek by family, the first of her line to learn Egyptian, and Rome’s rival.

facts.text: Cleopatra VII, born in 70 or 69 BCE, belonged to the Ptolemies, a royal family of Macedonian Greek descent.
Plutarch says the kings of Egypt before Cleopatra had not even tried to learn Egyptian, but she did, and she seldom needed an interpreter.
For political reasons Cleopatra styled herself the new Isis.
Cleopatra ruled from 51 to 30 BCE; forced out by her brother Ptolemy XIII, she regained power with Julius Caesar’s help and had a son by him, Caesarion.
Cleopatra later allied with Mark Antony; Octavian defeated them at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE, and she died in 30 BCE.
Legend says Cleopatra killed herself with an asp’s bite, but how she died is uncertain.
A coin from Cleopatra’s alliance with Antony shows both with beaked noses and jutting chins, like her Ptolemaic ancestors; the paired faces advertised their partnership.
Cleopatra’s mother is not known for certain, so part of her ancestry is uncertain.
Plutarch wrote that Cleopatra’s beauty was not in itself incomparable, but that her conversation had an irresistible charm.

title: Royal names and the cartouche
description: A pharaoh had five names; the throne and birth names were written in a protective oval called a cartouche.

facts.text: A pharaoh’s full title had five names, each introduced by a title: Horus, Two Ladies, Golden Horus, King of Upper and Lower Egypt, and Son of Re.
Of the king’s five names, one was given at birth and the other four at his coronation.
Two of the king’s names, the throne name and the birth name, were written inside an oval called a cartouche.
The cartouche shows a loop of rope and represents a shen ring, a circle symbolizing eternity, protecting the name inside.
The word cartouche is French for a paper cartridge; the ovals got the name because they looked like rolled paper cartridges.
“Ozymandias,” the Greek name for Ramesses II, comes from his throne name, Usermaatre.

title: The mummy’s curse
description: The curse of Tutankhamun’s tomb is a myth born of a mosquito bite, newspapers and older fiction.

facts.text: Howard Carter, who led the Tutankhamun excavation, died in London in 1939, aged 64.
Lord Carnarvon, Carter’s patron, died in Cairo in April 1923 of infection after a mosquito bite received while visiting the newly opened burial chamber.
Carnarvon’s death set off sensational newspaper stories about a mummy’s curse.
Mummy curses appeared in fiction long before, such as Louisa May Alcott’s 1869 story “Lost in a Pyramid; or, The Mummy’s Curse.”
A 2002 BMJ study compared Westerners exposed to the “curse” with those who were not: the exposed died at an average age of 70, with no significant difference, so no evidence of a curse.

title: Famous pharaohs compared
description: Egypt’s famous rulers owe their fame to different things: a pyramid, a tomb, building and spin, or Rome.

facts.text: Egypt’s famous rulers are famous for different reasons: Khufu for his pyramid, Tutankhamun for his tomb, Ramesses II for his building and self-promotion, Cleopatra for her struggle with Rome.

title: The Sea Peoples
description: Around 1177 BCE Ramesses III beat off the Sea Peoples, raiders of debated identity, but Egypt emerged diminished from the wider Late Bronze Age collapse.

facts.text: Historian Eric Cline dates the Sea Peoples’ attack on Egypt to 1177 BCE, the eighth year of Ramesses III’s reign; some attackers came by land and others by sea.
