Ramesses III defeated the Sea Peoples in battles on land and at sea, probably fought in or near the Nile Delta.
Ramesses III recorded the battles and rows of captured Sea Peoples on the walls of his mortuary temple at Medinet Habu, near Thebes.
Egyptian images show the Sea Peoples with different gear, from feathered headdresses to horned helmets, suggesting diverse groups from different places.
Egyptian texts name Sea Peoples groups such as the Peleset, generally believed to be the Philistines, and the Sherden, probably from Sardinia; their exact origins remain uncertain.

Scholars once blamed the Sea Peoples for destroying powers such as the Hittite empire; recent research sees the Late Bronze Age collapse as having many causes, including climate change, and their role is debated.
Egypt was the only major power to successfully resist the Sea Peoples, but afterward New Kingdom Egypt was much diminished in influence and power.

title: Priests and kings
description: After the New Kingdom, Egypt split: 21st Dynasty kings ruled the north from Tanis while the High Priests of Amun ruled the south from Thebes, rescuing robbed royal mummies.

facts.text: Herihor, high priest of Amun at Karnak in Thebes, took the full pharaonic title and founded a line of priest-kings that ruled southern Egypt as the country became disunited late in the 20th dynasty.
In the 21st Dynasty, kings ruled Lower Egypt from Tanis, in the Delta, while the High Priests of Amun in Thebes became more and more powerful.
Shoshenq, a Libyan leader, founded Egypt’s 22nd Dynasty, which governed from Tanis.
The Third Intermediate Period ended when the rulers of Kush, advancing from the south, took control of Egypt as its 25th Dynasty.
After the royal tombs at Thebes were robbed, 21st Dynasty priests and officials rewrapped damaged royal mummies and hid several New Kingdom kings in a cache at Deir el-Bahari to protect them.
The Deir el-Bahari cache was discovered in 1881, and the mummy and coffin of Ramesses II were among those found in it.

title: The Nubian pharaohs of Kush
description: Kush, a major Nubian civilization south of Egypt, conquered Egypt and ruled it as the 25th Dynasty, then carried on for about a thousand years more, building many pyramids.

facts.text: Kush was the southern part of the ancient region of Nubia, which extended from near the Nile’s first cataract south to about Khartoum, in what is now Sudan.
Kush was one of Africa’s earliest civilizations, and its kings ruled Egypt as the 25th Dynasty for nearly a century.
The Kushite kings ruled from Napata, near Mount Barkal, and the cult of the Egyptian god Amun was strongly rooted among the Kushites.
In the 8th century BCE the Kushite king Piye invaded Egypt, ended its petty kingdoms and took Memphis; by about 715 BCE, under Piye and then Shabaka, all of Egypt was ruled from Kush.
Piye recorded his conquest on a great stone stela that was found at Mount Barkal, where he returned with the spoils.
Kushite kings were buried in pyramids, and Sudan has some 255 ancient pyramids, more than twice as many as Egypt built.
After the Assyrians invaded Egypt in 671 BCE and defeated the army of the Kushite king Taharqa, the Kushites were driven back to Nubia by 654 BCE.
After leaving Egypt, Kush lasted about another thousand years, with its capital later moved south to Meroe, until the king of Aksum destroyed Meroe in 350 CE.

title: Persian rule
description: Persia conquered Egypt in 525 BCE; its kings ruled as pharaohs until a revolt restored native kings from 404 to 343 BCE, and Persian rule ended with Alexander in 332 BCE.

facts.text: In 525 BCE the Persian king Cambyses II won the Battle of Pelusium in the Nile Delta, took Memphis, and Egyptian resistance collapsed.
After conquering Egypt, Cambyses II had himself crowned as pharaoh.
The Persian king Darius I restored the Egyptian priests’ privileges, ordered a written codification of Egyptian law, and completed or repaired a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea.
Egypt was under Persian rule from 525 to 404 BCE, so Herodotus’s 5th-century BCE visit came while Egypt was Persian.
Herodotus accused Cambyses of many atrocities in Egypt and blamed them on madness, but contemporary Egyptian sources suggest his accusations must largely be discounted.
Egypt rebelled against Persia near the end of Darius I’s reign, and in 404 BCE it regained its independence under Amyrtaeus of Sais.
Nectanebo II, who reigned from 360 to 343 BCE, was the last native Egyptian king; when Persia reconquered Egypt in 343 BCE he fled south, and nothing more is known of him.
Egypt remained under Persian rule until 332 BCE, when the Persian satrap surrendered to Alexander the Great.

title: Alexander in Egypt
description: Alexander the Great took Egypt from Persia without a fight in 332 BCE, was crowned and hailed as son of Amun, founded Alexandria, and was buried there after his death.

facts.text: In November 332 BCE Alexander the Great, king of Macedonia, reached Egypt; the people welcomed him as their deliverer, and the Persian satrap Mazaces surrendered.
At Memphis, Alexander sacrificed to the sacred Apis bull and was crowned with the traditional double crown of the pharaohs.
At the oracle of Amun in the Siwa oasis, the priest greeted Alexander with the traditional salutation of a pharaoh, as son of Amun.
Alexander founded Alexandria near the western arm of the Nile, between the sea and Lake Mareotis, on a site protected by the island of Pharos.
Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BCE; his general Ptolemy diverted his body to Egypt, where it was eventually placed in a golden coffin in Alexandria.

title: Alexandria’s lighthouse and library
description: Alexandria, Egypt’s capital for nearly a thousand years, had the Pharos lighthouse and a library that tried to collect every book; the library declined gradually, for debated reasons.

facts.text: The lighthouse on the island of Pharos, built by Sostratus of Cnidus, was finished under Ptolemy II in about 280 BCE and was one of the Seven Wonders of the World.
The Pharos lighthouse was more than 110 metres high; the only taller human-made structures of its time would have been the pyramids of Giza.
According to ancient sources, a broad spiral ramp led to the top of the lighthouse, where a fire burned at night.
The lighthouse was destroyed by an earthquake in the 1300s, and in 1477 the sultan Qaitbay built a fort from its ruins.
Around 295 BCE, Ptolemy I charged Demetrius of Phaleron with founding the Library of Alexandria and the Mouseion, a research institute for scholars.
The Library aimed to gather all the books in the world, and books found on ships entering Alexandria were confiscated or copied for it.
At least part of the Library was damaged in 48 BCE during Julius Caesar’s civil war, but scholars seem to have kept working there afterward.
Historians describe the Library of Alexandria’s end as a slow decline through neglect and several blows over centuries, not a single fire, and its causes are still debated.
Modern historians call the story that Arab conquerors burned the Library of Alexandria a myth.

title: The Ptolemies
description: Ptolemy, Alexander’s Macedonian general, founded a dynasty that ruled Egypt for almost 300 years, presenting itself to Egyptians as pharaohs while keeping its own Greek ways.

facts.text: Ptolemy I, a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great, became satrap (governor) of Egypt after Alexander’s death in 323 BCE and proclaimed himself king in 305 BCE.
The Ptolemaic dynasty ruled Egypt from 305 BCE until Cleopatra VII’s death in 30 BCE; counted from Ptolemy’s start as governor in 323 BCE, that is almost 300 years.
The dynasty’s kings were all named Ptolemy, numbered from Ptolemy I to Ptolemy XV.
The Ptolemies supported Egyptian religious foundations and appeared on temple reliefs in the traditional pharaonic style.
Ptolemy I promoted Serapis, a god with Egyptian roots given many Greek features, whose cult fused Egyptian and Greek religion.
Manetho wrote his Greek history of Egypt around 300 BCE, early in the rule of the Ptolemies.
Ptolemy II married his full sister, Arsinoe II, which became a distinctive feature of the dynasty.
According to the ancient writer Plutarch, Cleopatra VII alone of the Ptolemies took the trouble to learn Egyptian.

title: Rome’s breadbasket
description: From 30 BCE Egypt was the Roman emperor’s own closely guarded province, and its Nile-fed grain helped feed the city of Rome.

facts.text: After 30 BCE, Octavian (the future emperor Augustus) treated Egypt as his own private kingdom, as heir of the Ptolemies, and it was run by a prefect appointed by the emperor.
Roman senators were forbidden to visit Egypt without the emperor’s permission.
Under Rome, Egypt’s granaries became Rome’s property, and Egypt became the breadbasket of the empire.
The historian Josephus, writing in the 1st century CE, said Egypt sent Rome enough grain to feed it for four months of the year, besides paying tribute in money.
Josephus noted that Egypt was walled round by almost impassable deserts, harborless seas and rivers, yet it still submitted to Rome.

title: The end of the old gods
description: Christianity spread through Egypt and the temples closed, the last at Philae in the 6th century; after the Arab conquest of 640 to 642 CE, Egypt became Muslim only gradually.

facts.text: Christianity is said to have been brought to Alexandria by St. Mark in the first half of the 1st century CE, and it spread quickly throughout Egypt.
The Copts, Egypt’s Christians, descend from pre-Islamic Egyptians who spoke Coptic, a late form of the Egyptian language.
In 391 CE Theophilus, the patriarch of Alexandria, and his followers destroyed the Serapeum at Alexandria, and other pagan temples were destroyed too, with Emperor Theodosius I’s encouragement.
The last known hieroglyphic inscription, carved at the temple of Philae, is dated 394 CE.
The Temple of Isis at Philae flourished in Roman times and was not closed until the reign of Justinian I (527 to 565 CE); late in his reign it was made into a church.
Arab forces under ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ defeated Byzantine armies in 640 and 641 CE and entered Alexandria, Egypt’s capital, in 642 CE.
Egypt was mostly Christian at the Arab conquest and became Muslim gradually over the following centuries; historians have no definite answer for when Muslims became the majority.
In the 12th century the Coptic church officially adopted Arabic for use alongside the Coptic language.

title: From pharaohs to foreign rulers
description: After the New Kingdom, Egypt passed from native pharaohs through Libyan, Kushite, Persian, Macedonian Greek, Roman and Arab rulers, most of whom presented themselves as pharaohs.

facts.text: After the New Kingdom, Egypt’s rulers included Libyans, Kushites, Persians, Macedonian Greeks, Romans and later Arabs, with a last spell of native kings from 404 to 343 BCE.

title: How hieroglyphs were forgotten
description: The last known hieroglyphs were carved in 394 CE; Egyptians switched to a Greek-based alphabet (Coptic), and later scholars like Horapollo misread the signs as symbols.

facts.text: From the last known hieroglyphic inscription in 394 CE to Champollion’s breakthrough in 1822, more than 1,400 years passed in which no one could read hieroglyphs.
The last known hieroglyphic inscription in Egypt was carved in 394 CE at the Temple of Isis at Philae; its signs are crude but still readable.
Hieroglyphs were still carved for more than four centuries after Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE, until 394 CE.
As Christianity spread in Egypt, Egyptians abandoned hieroglyphs for an adapted form of the Greek alphabet.
Coptic, the final stage of the ancient Egyptian language, was written in the Greek alphabet plus seven letters borrowed from demotic.
In the 5th century CE, the Greco-Egyptian scholar Horapollo wrote the Hieroglyphica, explaining hieroglyphs as symbols and allegories; he could not read them himself.
Horapollo’s Hieroglyphica was influential in the Renaissance, and the idea that hieroglyphs were symbols rather than sounds lasted until Champollion.

title: The Rosetta Stone
description: Found by French soldiers in 1799, the Rosetta Stone carries one decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, giving scholars a readable translation; it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

facts.text: The Rosetta Stone was found in 1799 by French soldiers of Napoleon’s campaign in Egypt, digging the foundations of a fort near the port of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta.
The Rosetta Stone carries the same decree three times: in hieroglyphs, in demotic (everyday Egyptian handwriting) and in ancient Greek, the language of Egypt’s Macedonian Greek rulers.
Scholars could still read ancient Greek, so the Greek text of the Rosetta Stone gave them a known translation of the Egyptian scripts.
The Rosetta Stone decree was issued in 196 BCE by priests of a temple in Memphis, confirming the Macedonian king Ptolemy V as a divine ruler.
After the French surrender in Egypt in 1801 the Rosetta Stone passed to the British; it has been on display in the British Museum since 1802, except when moved to safety in the First World War.

title: Champollion cracks hieroglyphs
description: Building on Thomas Young’s work on the name Ptolemy, Champollion showed in 1822 that hieroglyphs mix sound signs with signs for ideas, using Coptic and names like Ramesses.

facts.text: On 14 September 1822, Jean-Francois Champollion burst in on his brother, cried “Je tiens mon affaire!” (“I’ve got it!”) and collapsed in a faint.
Thomas Young, an English physicist also known for his work on light, began studying the Rosetta Stone’s texts in 1814.
Thomas Young showed that some hieroglyphs on the Rosetta Stone wrote the sounds of a royal name, Ptolemy, and he made major advances in reading demotic.
Champollion counted 1,419 hieroglyphic signs on the Rosetta Stone against 486 words in its Greek text, too many for each sign to be a whole idea.
Champollion showed that hieroglyphs were a mixed system: many signs stood for sounds, and others stood for whole ideas or objects.
Champollion knew Coptic, which helped him work out the sounds of hieroglyphs; with it he read the name of Ramesses, a native Egyptian king.
On 27 September 1822, Champollion announced his decipherment at the Academie des Inscriptions in Paris, with Thomas Young in the audience.

title: Egyptomania
description: Napoleon’s scholars and their Description de l’Egypte, then Champollion’s decipherment, set off a Western craze for Egyptian style, from buildings to obelisks shipped to London and New York.

facts.text: Napoleon’s 1798 invasion of Egypt was also the first large-scale scientific expedition to Egypt: he took about 150 artists, scientists, architects and printers.
The expedition’s record, the Description de l’Egypte, was published from 1809, with huge prints of the pyramids, temples and other antiquities.
The Description and Champollion’s 1822 decipherment fed a craze for Egyptian art and style in Europe and America known as Egyptomania.
Architects copied Egyptian designs from the Description; in the United States the first wave was mostly buildings, including cemetery architecture and the Washington Monument, begun in 1848.
Two granite obelisks carved about 3,500 years ago for Thutmose III were given away by Egypt’s government: one was raised in London in 1878, the other in New York’s Central Park in 1881.
The obelisks are called Cleopatra’s Needles because the Romans moved them to Alexandria and set them up at the Caesarium, a temple conceived by Cleopatra.

title: Finding Tutankhamun’s tomb
description: Funded by Lord Carnarvon, Howard Carter found Tutankhamun’s largely intact tomb in November 1922 and spent about ten years recording its 5,398 objects.

facts.text: Lord Carnarvon had funded Howard Carter’s digging for years with little to show; in 1922 Carter persuaded him to pay for one final season, which began on 1 November.
On 4 November 1922, Carter’s team found a step cut into the bedrock under the remains of ancient workmen’s huts, about four metres below the entrance of Ramesses VI’s tomb.
After exposing a sealed doorway, Carter cabled Carnarvon in England: “At last have made wonderful discovery in Valley.”

On 26 November 1922, Carter looked through a second sealed doorway, stamped with Tutankhamun’s seals, by candlelight; when Carnarvon asked if he could see anything, his journal says he replied “Yes, it is wonderful.”
Carter’s later popular account gave his reply as the famous line “Yes, wonderful things.”
Tutankhamun’s tomb was found largely intact, the first known intact royal burial from ancient Egypt.
Carter’s team numbered the 5,398 objects found in Tutankhamun’s tomb and spent about ten years clearing and recording them.
The excavation’s notes, photographs and drawings are kept at the Griffith Institute, University of Oxford.

title: Studying Egypt today
description: Muon scans find hidden spaces in the Great Pyramid, CT scans unwrap mummies digitally, and infrared satellite images reveal buried buildings.

facts.text: Muons are particles made when cosmic rays hit the atmosphere and constantly rain down; stone absorbs some of them, so detectors can map empty spaces inside a pyramid.
In 2017, the ScanPyramids team reported a big void at least 30 metres long above the Grand Gallery of the Great Pyramid, found with muons.
In 2023, muon scans located a corridor about 9 metres long behind the Great Pyramid’s north face, and a camera pushed inside confirmed it.
Amenhotep I’s mummy, so finely wrapped with garlands and a mask that it was never opened in modern times, was digitally unwrapped with CT scans in 2021 by Sahar Saleem and Zahi Hawass.
The CT scans showed Amenhotep I was about 35 when he died, had good teeth and was buried with 30 amulets inside his wrappings.

Sarah Parcak of the University of Alabama at Birmingham processes satellite images to see in infrared, invisible to the human eye; in the desert they show moisture differences above buried mud bricks.
Parcak’s team mapped the street grid of Tanis, once a capital in the Nile Delta, and tracked tomb looting after 2011.

title: Who owns the past?
description: Egyptian voices such as Zahi Hawass call for the return of the Rosetta Stone and the Nefertiti bust; the British Museum and Berlin’s museum argue they were acquired lawfully; Egypt opened the Grand Egyptian Museum in 2025.

facts.text: In 2022, Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, launched a petition for the Rosetta Stone’s return that passed 100,000 signatures.
Hawass also calls for the return of the bust of Nefertiti from Berlin and the Dendera Zodiac from the Louvre, saying these unique objects belong in Egypt.
Hawass argues that the bust of Nefertiti, found in 1912 and taken to Berlin in 1913, left Egypt illegally.

The British Museum says the Rosetta Stone came to Britain under an 1801 treaty signed by a representative of Egypt, notes that Egypt’s government has made no formal request, and that 21 of the 28 known copies of the decree are in Egypt.
Berlin’s museum points out that the Nefertiti bust left Egypt through an official division of finds in 1913, overseen by an inspector of Egypt’s antiquities service.
The Grand Egyptian Museum, near the Great Pyramid at Giza, officially opened on 1 November 2025 with about 100,000 artifacts.
At the Grand Egyptian Museum, Tutankhamun’s entire collection is shown together for the first time since its discovery.

title: Myths about Egypt
description: Evidence answers popular myths: paid workers, not slaves, built the Giza pyramids; builders’ records like Merer’s logbook leave no room for aliens; the curse and Cleopatra’s looks are shakier than their fame.

facts.text: Howard Carter, who opened Tutankhamun’s tomb in 1922, lived until 1939.
The idea that slaves built the pyramids comes from the Greek historian Herodotus, misreadings of the biblical book of Exodus and Hollywood films.
Near the Giza pyramids, archaeologists found workers’ districts with bakeries and workshops, and workers’ tombs close to the pyramids, some naming the dead; most now think paid laborers built them.
In 2013, archaeologists at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea found the oldest known inscribed papyri, including the logbook of an official named Merer.
Merer’s logbook records his crew shipping limestone by boat from the Tura quarries to Giza for Khufu’s pyramid, in half-day entries.
Cleopatra belonged to a Macedonian Greek dynasty, but her mother’s identity is uncertain, and her coins and portrait busts do not all agree.
Plutarch wrote that Cleopatra’s beauty was “not altogether incomparable,” but that conversation with her had “an irresistible charm.”

title: Egypt’s legacy
description: Our calendar descends from Egypt’s solar calendar via Julius Caesar, the letter A from an ox-head sign, and the word paper from papyrus.

facts.text: In 46 BCE Julius Caesar reformed Rome’s calendar by adopting the Egyptian solar calendar, advised by Sosigenes of Alexandria: 365 and a quarter days, with an extra day every fourth year.
Pope Gregory XIII fine-tuned Caesar’s calendar in 1582, and the Gregorian calendar gradually replaced the Julian one.

The letter A goes back to a sign shaped like an ox’s head: early Semitic writing in Sinai adopted it around 1500 BCE, the Phoenicians called it aleph (“ox”), and the Greeks renamed it alpha and used it for a vowel.
The inventors of the alphabet were influenced by Egyptian writing; inscriptions from Sinai show a stage between Egyptian hieroglyphs and the Semitic alphabet.
The word “paper” comes from papyrus, the Egyptian writing material, which the Greeks adopted and the Roman Empire used widely.
Books and documents on papyrus were still made, sporadically, until about the 12th century.
